Seven miz men, one man:
If they beat you, will they leave your carcass?
Restrain your son and heed my words;
That is what I say—understand it!”
When he had finished speaking,
Rich Jakyp's senior wife,
The renowned Chyyrdy,
From her quail-like black eyes
Now shed tears in drops.
The noble woman Chyyrdy,
Her white breasts showing,
Her white throat peeping out,
Spoke quietly and said:
“You had much livestock but no child;
In longing we were granted Manas.
We were driven out of Altai,
Lamenting without a camel calf.
Your spring in the valley,
This son of yours named Manas,
Your darling granted at death's door,
Your tender mottled-gray goshawk,
Your only Manas whom you were granted,
Your gray hawk, your morning star.
You lamented, having no child;
Whom have you apart from Manas?!
Your only Manas whom you were granted,
Who lets no bustard escape on the plain,
My mottled-gray falcon Manas,
Who will not stay on the mountain peak,
He was a black-and-white female falcon.
You were the master who held him,
Your spring flowing from the hills,
Your generous darling Manas.
He is the marked one, he your support,
Against an enemy who faces him
He is the lion who raises uproar.
Do not grieve, rich Jakyp;
Your only Manas is your lion.
He is the marked one, he your support,
Created by the great Almighty,
He is a lion beyond other mortals.
When Manas was conceived,
Raided and scattered though we were,
I cast off all my sorrow.
When the craving for the child came,
I craved a lion.
There is a reason for his birth;
There is much to tell if I speak.
The black ridge you lean upon—
Is Manas not your support?
Who will scatter your countless herds—
Is that not your lion Manas?
He came to you from the unseen,
Your only son Manas,
Found after repeated lamenting.
The two eyes that keep watching—
Is Manas not their tears?
The aching breast—
Is Manas not its pain?
Your Manas granted at death's door,
If he grows to be a mighty man,
If he equals a hero's son,
When his calves fill out,
When he wins the name of champion,
He will fulfill his wishes:
‘My son has turned out unruly,’
Do not lament over your livestock.
Every one of your chests
He will fill with treasures of yellow gold.
Your yurt felt will drip with fat;
If your only son survives,
He will make you khan in every quarter.
What was severed will be joined;
If your son Manas is there,
What was scattered will be gathered.
Turn your mind toward honesty;
May God bring you back,
Never sated by asking for food,
Never abandoning greed—
May God return you
To your dear Kyrgyz people.
How can our sorrow be eased?
Your seven dear kinsmen,
From these Chinese people's cruelty,
Were driven away and lost.
Those seven went away;
Their names unheard, they are absent.
Do not grieve, rich Jakyp.
Wailing, we were parted from our people.
The one you sit relying on—
Unless it is your only Manas,
How shall we see those people again?
If your Manas survives,
He will find the lands of Keng-Kol and Talas.
‘The inheritance my father left,’ he will say,
And find the Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
If your Manas survives,
Your sorrowful brow will clear;
Your burning heart will be soothed.
For these worthless, faithless livestock,
Saying, ‘My son has turned out unruly,’
Do not trouble yourself and grieve.
Your only Manas belongs to good fortune;
These livestock you raised with such toil,
When the wind howls, belong to disaster.
Your Manas granted at death's door
Was born here in Altai.
If he survives, you will see:
In Beijing with its kakan,
If he lives, he will raise uproar.
There is a reason he will raise uproar:
When he had just been born,
He landed upright on his feet.
When I looked behind him,
A gray wolf's mane spilled down.
When I opened the hem of my dress,
A lion's form appeared.
While he lay in his birth membrane,
Twelve old women saw him.
‘Rich Jakyp's senior wife
Has given birth to a calamity,’ they said,
And the twelve old women died.
When he came down upon the earth,
He roared in wrath.
To send news to those who knew,
He cried the battle cry ‘Manas!’
His signs were these:
His ears were pierced,
His foreskin circumcised.
When he cried he recited the creed;
This was his true appearance.
His body reached the earth,
Low mist descended and hail fell;
Throughout the land of Altai
An earthquake passed.
When she gave birth to Manas,
Drenched in blood,
Unable to bear it, the poor soul,
Chyyrdy suffered in travail.
‘It was Kydyr himself,’ I say;
To this day I marvel.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
A white-bearded dervish
Stroked his forehead three times.
The dervish stood and said:
‘Do not grieve, woman;
Your heavy sorrow has been eased.
A lion has come into your hands;
Now your heart has opened.
Drinking blood, he will grow hardened;
Slaughtering many unbelievers,
He will be called Bloodthirsty Manas.
He will break rock and make a road,
Destroying many,
Attacking many lands.
No mortal will dare face him;
No enemy will defeat him face to face.
If an enemy has the strength of an army,
He will join with the forty chiltens.
Making his dun horse lumber along,
He will lead twelve choro.
God has given you
Your valiant son Manas.
If an armed enemy appears,
Will one who faces him remain alive?
When Manas grows up safe and well,
He will cut through forest and make a road.
Where ears have heard and eyes have seen,
He will attack throughout the world.
He will enter the caliph’s presence and receive a letter,
Giving his hand to twelve spiritual guides;
He himself will be called zayypurush.
This son of yours now born
Is the youngest of six lions,
Allah's beloved servant.
His world is in balance;
If you look within him,
He is broader than the face of the earth.
No man will bring him harm;
In the eighteen thousand worlds,
None remains to turn a lasso-pole against him.
High-browed, bright-faced,
He will lay flat whoever challenges him.
His world is in balance;
He is the lion supported by Shay.
Your son will grow up safe and well,
Herding white deer, making them cattle.
All who shoot at him
He will drive before him and confound.
If this son of yours grows up,
He will be a towering black mountain.
If he attacks in wrath,
How can an enemy stay unharmed?
This is the splendid lion Manas.’
These were the dervish's words:
‘Forty champions will come to Manas,
All forty from forty different origins.
The inept call them forty choro;
They are not forty choro but forty companions.
All forty from forty different origins,
The forty champions, foremost across the ages.
When horses grow fat and fit,
The companions of this son
Will come from afar and number forty.
When he reaches twelve,
He will gird his wrathful waist.
The Black Kalmyks and Chinese
He will attack and make recoil.
He will break courts and take spoils,
Attack mighty lands,
Raise dust with his tread,
Take lives with his voice.’
When he was an infant,
The dervish told him this.
Having spoken, that man
Vanished from sight.
Sent by the Creator,
It was a deed that gave a sign.
That man's name was Kydyr,
Peace be upon him himself.
If you observe Manas,
It was the time he blessed him.
It was Kydyr himself,
Not just himself, but his very eye.
To be a companion to Manas,
That was when he came to meet him.
When I heard that man's words,
From joy, my poor soul,
My heart became burning coals.
The man who was speaking
Vanished and was gone from sight.
Do not grieve for livestock, Jakyp;
Will the child not spend what you gathered?
Do not put your trust in livestock
Unless support comes from your child.
You cannot sate your longing by looking;
The child you were granted through lament,
Your black-marked tynar hawk,
This year, if God wills,
Will reach the age to wage holy war.
When you count the days,
When you reckon the time,
This year your Manas
Has reached twelve;
This very year your darling
Has become twelve years old.
‘My son has turned out unruly,’
Do not grieve for your livestock;
Give courage to your child.
If you do not give your child courage,
There is Kanggay at your flank;
In Kanggay are Black Kalmyks.
Take courage, do not grieve;
There is a burden to fall on you.
